lead: At high power the refractive index of silica rises with the light intensity. A pulse then changes its own phase as it travels, a chirp that widens its spectrum: self-phase modulation (SPM). When the fiber has anomalous dispersion, that chirp can cancel the dispersion broadening exactly, and the pulse travels unchanged as a soliton. Only a few syllabi teach this topic. SPM sets the power ceiling of a WDM channel, and solitons show how nonlinearity and dispersion can be made to work together.
prereq: You need: chromatic dispersion and the group-velocity dispersion β₂ (see Chromatic dispersion: material and waveguide) and fiber attenuation in dB/km (see Attenuation in optical fibers).

sections.h3: The Kerr effect and the nonlinear length

blocks.text: Silica is not perfectly linear. Its refractive index follows the light intensity: n = n₀ + n₂I. Here n₀ is the low-power index, I is the intensity in W/m², and n₂ is the Kerr coefficient, about 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W for silica. The change is tiny, but a long fiber adds it up.

The intensity is not uniform across the mode, so one number, the effective area A<sub>eff</sub>, stands for the mode size (about 80 µm² in standard single-mode fiber). The nonlinear coefficient is γ = 2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>). With λ in m, A<sub>eff</sub> in m² and n₂ in m²/W, γ comes out in W⁻¹m⁻¹; multiply by 1000 for W⁻¹km⁻¹, the usual unit, typically 1 to 3 W⁻¹km⁻¹. The nonlinear length L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀) is the distance over which the nonlinear phase reaches 1 rad for a peak power P₀.

A lossy fiber weakens the light as it goes, so the nonlinearity acts over an effective length L<sub>eff</sub> = (1 − e<sup>−αL</sup>)/α, with α the loss in 1/km (α = loss in dB/km ÷ 4.343). For a long span L<sub>eff</sub> is close to 1/α, about 21.7 km at 0.2 dB/km.

A pulse carries its own index change, so it phase-modulates itself. The nonlinear phase is φ<sub>NL</sub> = γP(T)L<sub>eff</sub>, largest at the pulse peak. A changing phase means a shifted frequency, δω = −dφ<sub>NL</sub>/dT. On the leading edge the power rises (dP/dT > 0), so δω is negative: a red shift. On the trailing edge the power falls, so the shift is to the blue. The pulse acquires a chirp without any modulator, and its spectrum widens while its shape is unchanged at first.

This is the practical limit on power per WDM channel. Push more power into one channel and its widened spectrum spills towards its neighbours, and with dispersion the chirp turns into distortion. EDFAs (Optical amplifiers) make these powers easy to reach in every span.

sections.h3: Solitons and the nonlinear Schrödinger equation

blocks.text: With dispersion the pulse envelope A(z,T) obeys the nonlinear Schrödinger equation (NLS): ∂A/∂z + (α/2)A + (iβ₂/2)∂²A/∂T² = iγ|A|²A. Here z is distance, T is time in a frame moving with the pulse, α is the loss, β₂ is the group-velocity dispersion and the right side is SPM. Read the terms rather than solving it: loss, dispersion and nonlinearity act together.

Two lengths compete. The dispersion length L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂| is the distance over which dispersion broadens a pulse of width parameter T₀. The soliton order N is set by N² = L<sub>D</sub>/L<sub>NL</sub>. In anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0, where higher frequencies travel faster) the blue trailing edge catches up and the red leading edge falls back, so the SPM chirp undoes the dispersion. When N = 1 the balance is exact: the fundamental soliton has a sech-shaped amplitude (sech² intensity), FWHM = 1.763 T₀, peak power P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²), and keeps its shape at every distance while its phase grows steadily. Higher-order solitons (N = 2, 3, …) narrow, split and recover their shape after the soliton period z₀ = (π/2)L<sub>D</sub>. Soliton systems were demonstrated over thousands of kilometres with amplifiers, but installed long-haul links use dispersion management and coherent detection instead.

examples.question: A fiber has β₂ = −20 ps²/km and γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹. A sech pulse has T₀ = 10 ps, so its FWHM is 1.763 T₀ = 17.6 ps. (a) Find L<sub>D</sub>. (b) Find the peak power of the fundamental soliton. (c) Check that L<sub>NL</sub> = L<sub>D</sub>. (d) Find the soliton period.
steps: P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²) = 20/(2 × 100) = 0.1 W = 100 mW. The units: ps²/km ÷ (W⁻¹km⁻¹ × ps²) = W.
L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀) = 1/(2 × 0.1) = 5 km, so N² = 5/5 = 1, the fundamental soliton.
Check: without the nonlinearity this sech pulse would be 1.54 times wider after 5 km and 2.14 times wider after 10 km (Figure 6.4.1); the soliton stays at 17.6 ps.
examples.answer: L<sub>D</sub> = 5 km, P₀ = 0.1 W (100 mW), L<sub>NL</sub> = 5 km so N = 1, and z₀ = 7.85 km.

examples.question: A standard fiber has n₂ = 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W, A<sub>eff</sub> = 80 µm² and a loss of 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm. One WDM channel of 10 mW is launched into an 80 km span. Find γ, L<sub>eff</sub>, the peak SPM phase and the power at which this phase reaches 1 rad.
steps: Check: L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP) = 1/(1.317 × 0.010) = 75.9 km at 10 mW, much longer than L<sub>eff</sub>, so SPM in one span is weak at this power.
examples.answer: γ = 1.32 W⁻¹km⁻¹, L<sub>eff</sub> = 21.17 km, φ<sub>NL</sub> = 0.279 rad at 10 mW, and the phase reaches 1 rad at about 35.9 mW.

traps: Using average power in γP₀ instead of the peak power P₀. For a short pulse the average power is much smaller, so the nonlinearity is badly underestimated.
Forgetting the sign of β₂. A bright soliton needs anomalous dispersion, β₂ < 0; with normal dispersion the SPM chirp and the dispersion chirp add and the pulse spreads faster.
Writing z₀ = L<sub>D</sub>. The soliton period is (π/2)L<sub>D</sub>, about 1.571 L<sub>D</sub>, and it is the period of the higher-order solitons; the fundamental soliton never changes shape.
Putting λ in nm or A<sub>eff</sub> in µm² into γ = 2πn₂/(λA<sub>eff</sub>) without converting. Use metres, then multiply W⁻¹m⁻¹ by 1000 for W⁻¹km⁻¹.

quiz.q: State the Kerr relation for the refractive index and give n₂ for silica.
quiz.a: n = n₀ + n₂I, with n₂ ≈ 2.6 × 10⁻²⁰ m²/W.

quiz.q: Define the nonlinear length L<sub>NL</sub> and the dispersion length L<sub>D</sub>.
quiz.a: L<sub>NL</sub> = 1/(γP₀), with P₀ the peak power; L<sub>D</sub> = T₀²/|β₂|.

quiz.q: Why does self-phase modulation widen the spectrum?
quiz.a: The phase follows the power, so δω = −dφ<sub>NL</sub>/dT: the rising edge shifts to the red and the falling edge to the blue, creating new frequencies on both sides.

quiz.q: A fiber has γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹ and a peak power of 0.5 W. Find L<sub>NL</sub>.
Find the fundamental-soliton peak power for T₀ = 5 ps, β₂ = −20 ps²/km and γ = 2 W⁻¹km⁻¹.
quiz.a: P₀ = |β₂|/(γT₀²) = 20/(2 × 25) = 0.4 W. Halving T₀ raises P₀ four times, and L<sub>D</sub> = 25/20 = 1.25 km.

quiz.q: Why does a bright soliton need anomalous dispersion?
quiz.a: SPM puts red on the leading edge and blue on the trailing edge. In anomalous dispersion (β₂ < 0) blue travels faster than red, so the trailing edge catches up and the leading edge falls back, which undoes the broadening. In normal dispersion (β₂ > 0) red is faster, the two effects push the same way, and the pulse spreads faster than by dispersion alone.

beyond: Not for the exam. Soliton transmission was tested in the 1990s over thousands of kilometres of amplified fiber, and soliton ideas still guide pulse shaping in fiber lasers. Kerr nonlinearity also generates supercontinuum light in photonic-crystal fiber and frequency combs in microresonators, and coherent systems now compensate part of SPM digitally. Search for optical soliton transmission, Kerr frequency comb and digital back-propagation.

Bottom: with only dispersion the worked example’s 17.6 ps pulse is 1.54 times wider at L<sub>D</sub> = 5 km and 2.14 times at 10 km; at the soliton power of 100 mW it keeps its width.

Bottom: a plot of width ratio against distance from 0 to 20 km, a rising curve through 1.54 at 5 km and 2.14 at 10 km, and a flat line at 1 for the soliton.
